cards.title: Rate factors: pressure only counts for gaseous reactants; explain with collisions per unit time

walkthrough.question:
Aqueous hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H2O2(aq) → 2H2O(l) + O2(g). Which changes make this reaction faster?
I. Adding a catalyst
II. Using a more concentrated H2O2(aq) solution
III. Raising the pressure
A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
walkthrough.key_idea: Pressure changes rate only when a reactant is a gas.
walkthrough.careful: Check the reactants' state symbols before accepting pressure.
procedure: Write down the state of each reactant.
Catalyst: alternative pathway with lower Ea, so faster.
Higher concentration: more frequent collisions, so faster.
Higher pressure: faster only if a reactant is gaseous.
Higher temperature: more particles with E ≥ Ea.
tricks: A gaseous product does not count: pressure needs a gaseous reactant.
Surface area matters only when a solid reactant is involved.
if_lost: What state is H2O2 in here?
Which particles does pressure actually push closer together?
Does a gas formed as a product affect collisions between reactant particles?

1_context.short: AO2: apply the rate factors to one stated reaction.
1_context.why: R2.2.3 lists pressure as a factor, but it works only by raising the concentration of gas particles. The exam checks whether you test that against this reaction.
1_context.avoid: Treating the syllabus list of factors as true for every reaction.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.3: pressure, concentration, surface area, temperature and catalysts influence rate.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach pressure using all-gas examples. The exam hides a solution reaction that gives off a gaseous product.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only I and II are right, so the answer is A.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Pressure raises collision frequency only for gas particles. The only reactant is aqueous, so pressure leaves its collisions unchanged.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Choosing D because O2 is a gas: 30% did this (25M.1A.HL.6213.25 report).
trigger_phrases: catalyst: alternative pathway with lower Ea
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Pressure counts only for gaseous reactants. A gaseous product never qualifies.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A versus D comes down to one thing: whether you checked that no reactant is a gas.

3_novel_application.short: The gaseous product O2 tempts you into picking pressure.
3_novel_application.why: Rate depends on collisions between reactant particles. O2 is only formed, so squeezing it does nothing to how often H2O2 particles collide.
3_novel_application.avoid: Reasoning that 'there is a gas in the equation', so pressure matters.
3_novel_application.disguise: A gas appears in the equation, but only on the product side.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask which reactant particles get closer together when the pressure rises.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: judge each numbered statement on its own.
4_command_terms.why: In I/II/III options, one false statement removes every option that contains it. Judging the statements one by one is faster than comparing whole options.
4_command_terms.avoid: Picking 'all three' because each factor sounds familiar.
4_command_terms.demands: Decide for this reaction whether each of I, II and III increases the rate.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 1 mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Check states first, then strike out III.
5_time_efficiency.why: Only option A leaves out III, so once pressure is ruled out the answer is fixed.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Weighing up I and II at length when III decides it.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No need to think further about I or II once III is out.

6_data_booklet.short: The booklet does not help; the state symbols are the data.
6_data_booklet.why: Collision theory and rate factors are not in the data booklet.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the booklet for rate factors.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None. Read the state symbols in the given equation.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The five rate factors, and that pressure acts only through the concentration of a gaseous reactant.

7_elimination.short: III is false, which removes B, C and D.
7_elimination.why: Every option except A includes pressure, so one check settles it.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping D because I and II are both correct.

definitely_wrong.rule: Contains III, but no reactant is a gas.
Contains III, but no reactant is a gas.
Contains III, but no reactant is a gas.

walkthrough.answer: A. A catalyst and a higher concentration both increase the rate. The only reactant is aqueous, so pressure has no effect.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.2–R2.2.4: collisions need enough energy and the right orientation; rate factors; Ea is the minimum energy for a successful collision.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books list the factors. Exams ask which factors apply to a given reaction, and they want precise collision-theory wording when you explain.

trigger_phrases: more frequent collisions / more collisions per unit time
trap_boundaries: 'More collisions' with no time reference loses the mark (24N.2.HL.TZ0.4 markscheme; 25M.2.HL.6221.8 markscheme; 24M.2.SL.TZ2.5).
Defining Ea without 'minimum' loses the mark (13M.2.SL.TZ2.2; 12N.2.HL.TZ0.6).
'Not enough energy' is too vague: say the collision energy is less than Ea (25M.2.SL.TZ2.3; 25M.2.HL.6215.3).
For temperature, examiners want more particles with E ≥ Ea, not only more collisions (03M.2.SL.TZ0.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit names the factor. Full credit links it to collisions per unit time and to the proportion of particles with E ≥ Ea.

disguises: A solution reaction with a gaseous product, used as pressure bait (25M.1A.HL.6213.25).
'What decides whether a collision leads to reaction': only energy and orientation, not concentration (08M.1.SL.TZ0.19).
Lower pressure at constant volume means a lower gas concentration (19M.2.HL.TZ2.2).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Separate what changes a single collision (energy, orientation) from what changes how often collisions happen (concentration, pressure, surface area).

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Explain items give one mark per collision-theory point from a list, for example 3 max: more kinetic energy, more frequent collisions, more particles with E ≥ Ea (25M.2.HL.6221.8).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Don't describe the experiment or restate the question.

6_data_booklet.hack: Collision theory, rate factors and the definition of Ea are NOT in the booklet: memorise them.

rules: Pressure has no effect if no reactant is a gas.
A catalyst never increases the kinetic energy of the particles.
Concentration and pressure change collision frequency, not the fraction of particles with E ≥ Ea. Only temperature (shifts the curve) or a catalyst (lowers Ea) change that fraction.

evidence.note: Answer A: catalyst and concentration; pressure is irrelevant for an aqueous reactant.
51% correct; 30% thought pressure increased the rate with no gaseous reactant.
Temperature explanation: more KE, more frequent collisions, more particles with E ≥ Ea; M2 needs a time reference.
'More collisions' is not accepted for M2.
Unsuccessful collision: wrong orientation, or energy less than Ea.
'Not enough energy' judged vague.
About 36% correct on which factors decide whether a collision reacts.
'More collisions' written instead of 'more frequent collisions'.
Marks lost for leaving 'minimum' out of the Ea definition.
Few linked lower pressure at constant volume to lower concentration.
59% correct on a pressure-and-rate MCQ.

cards.difficulty_signal: 51% correct on 25M.1A.HL.6213.25, with 30% wrongly including pressure. 'Factors affecting rate', 'effect of pressure' and 'connecting rate explanation with time' were flagged difficult in May 2025.

cards.title: Measuring rate: name a changing property and measure it against time

walkthrough.question: Nitrogen dioxide, NO2, is a brown gas. It forms from nitrogen monoxide and oxygen: 2NO(g) + O2(g) → 2NO2(g). Suggest a way to measure the rate of this reaction. [1]
walkthrough.key_idea: Name a property that changes AND measure it against time.
walkthrough.question_type: Suggest a method to measure rate
walkthrough.careful: Always add 'with time' or 'per unit time'.
procedure: Find what changes: colour, gas amount, mass or pH.
Pick one property you can measure for this reaction.
Add a condition: constant volume or constant pressure.
Say it is measured at regular time intervals.
tricks: Count moles of gas: 3 become 2, so pressure falls.
A coloured reactant or product means a colorimeter will work.
if_lost: Which species in the equation is coloured?
Does the number of moles of gas change from left to right?
Besides a property, what else must a rate measurement include?

1_context.short: AO2: pick a measurable property for this reaction.
1_context.why: R2.2.1 defines rate as change per unit time. The mark tests both parts: a property, and time.
1_context.avoid: Naming a property without any mention of time.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.1: rate is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show the apparatus (gas syringe, balance). The exam wants you to choose a property from the equation and phrase it as a change with time.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Colour, pressure or volume, each changing with time.
2_markscheme_logic.why: A rate is a change per unit time. A single reading gives an amount, not a rate.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Leaving out time: the mean mark was 0.37/1 for this reason (24N.2.HL.TZ0.6 report).
trigger_phrases: change in «gas» pressure «at constant volume» with time
change in «gas» volume «at constant pressure» with time
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: No mark for a change stated without reference to time.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: 'The colour changes' scores 0. 'Change in colour measured over time' scores 1.

3_novel_application.short: An all-gas smog reaction: no precipitate, no mass loss.
3_novel_application.why: Choose from what the equation offers: a brown product and a fall in the number of gas moles.
3_novel_application.avoid: Suggesting pH change or titration, which was rejected for a similar gas reaction (25M.2.HL.6215.3 markscheme).
3_novel_application.disguise: An atmospheric reaction instead of a familiar lab set-up.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Scan the equation for colour, a change in gas moles, ions or solids.

4_command_terms.short: Suggest: give one workable method, briefly.
4_command_terms.why: Suggest accepts any valid proposal. One correct method that includes time scores the mark.
4_command_terms.avoid: Listing several methods when one of them is wrong.
4_command_terms.demands: Propose one property that changes and can be measured over time.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 1 mark, all or nothing; any one accepted method.

5_time_efficiency.short: One line: the property plus 'with time'.
5_time_efficiency.why: It is worth one mark, so it deserves about 20 seconds.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing out a full practical method.
workflow: Spot the colour or gas change
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No apparatus diagram or step-by-step procedure.

6_data_booklet.short: The booklet does not help; read the equation.
6_data_booklet.why: Practical methods and colours of species are not in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for colours in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None. The colour given in the stem and the state symbols are the data.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Methods for following rate: colorimetry, gas volume, pressure, mass loss, conductivity.

7_elimination.short: Rule out any answer that leaves out time.
7_elimination.why: The time phrase is the most common reason this mark is lost, so check it first.

definitely_wrong.target: A property with no time reference
definitely_wrong.rule: It gives an amount, not a rate, so it is not accepted.
No acid or base changes in this gas reaction (rejected in 25M.2.HL.6215.3).
In a closed all-gas system nothing escapes, so the mass stays constant.

walkthrough.answer: Measure the change in brown colour (for example with a colorimeter) over time. Also accepted: the change in pressure at constant volume, or in volume at constant pressure, over time.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.1: rate as change per unit time; rates from tangents to concentration, volume or mass–time graphs.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books define rate. Exams ask how to follow it in a given reaction and how to read a rate from the tangent at a stated time.

trigger_phrases: change in X with time / per unit time
at constant volume / at constant pressure
gradient of the tangent at time t
trap_boundaries: A property with no time reference scores 0 (24N.2.HL.TZ0.6).
pH change or titrating is not accepted for phosgene formation (25M.2.HL.6215.3).
An average rate over the first interval is not the rate at a point: draw the tangent (12M.2.HL.TZ2.1; 12M.2.SL.TZ2.1; 24M.2.HL.TZ2.6).
When the question asks for the initial rate from the graph, a rate-equation calculation scores nothing (24M.2.SL.TZ2.5).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit names a property. Full credit gives the property, a time reference and, for gases, the condition held constant.

disguises: Rate in unusual units such as mm s−1 read from a graph (12M.2.SL.TZ2.1).
Reaction followed by the time a colour takes to change (25M.2.HL.6209.6).
Explaining why rate falls over time: concentration drops, so collisions become less frequent (04M.2.SL.TZ0.1).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Rate is a slope. A single value at a single time is never a rate.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: A method is 1 mark. A rate from a graph is typically 3 marks: tangent drawn, gradient worked out, value in the accepted range (19M.3.SL.TZ2.2).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Don't average from the origin, and don't use the rate equation when the graph is asked for.

6_data_booklet.hack: The rate definition and practical methods are NOT in the booklet. Section 1 gives n = CV and PV = nRT if you need to turn a volume or pressure into moles.

rules: Any answer without a time reference is wrong.
An average rate measured from the origin is not the instantaneous rate at a later time.
Mass loss works only if a gas escapes from an open container.

evidence.note: Part (a)(i): suggest a method to measure the rate of NO2 formation.
Accepted answers: colour, pressure or volume change, each with time. Changes without time are rejected.
Mean 0.37/1: the mark was lost by not taking repeated readings at different times.
Pressure or volume change per unit time accepted; pH change or titration rejected.
Methods often lacked 'at different times'.
Few saw that the rate is the gradient of the tangent at 120 s; many gave average rates.
Initial rate taken from the data instead of from a tangent.
Marks given for the tangent, the gradient calculation and a reasonable final value.

cards.difficulty_signal: Mean 0.37/1 on 24N.2.HL.TZ0.6(a)(i). 'How to monitor the rate of a reaction' was flagged difficult in May 2018, and tangent errors recur in 2012, 2019 and 2024 reports.

cards.title: Orders from initial-rate data: hold one concentration fixed, vary the other

walkthrough.question:
For 2NO(g) + O2(g) → 2NO2(g), initial rates were measured:
Exp 1: [NO] = 0.020 mol dm−3, [O2] = 0.010 mol dm−3, rate = 0.028 mol dm−3 s−1
Exp 2: [NO] = 0.020 mol dm−3, [O2] = 0.020 mol dm−3, rate = 0.057 mol dm−3 s−1
Exp 3: [NO] = 0.040 mol dm−3, [O2] = 0.020 mol dm−3, rate = 0.227 mol dm−3 s−1
Determine the order with respect to each reactant and write the rate expression. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: Change one concentration; the factor the rate changes by gives the order.
walkthrough.question_type: Orders and rate equation from rate data
walkthrough.careful: Use a pair of experiments where only one concentration changes.
procedure: Find two runs where only one concentration changes.
Work out the concentration factor and the rate factor.
Rate factor 1 → order 0; same factor → 1; factor squared → 2.
Repeat for every species in the table, catalysts too.
Write rate = k[...] with each order as the exponent.
tricks: Concentration ×2 with rate ×1, ×2 or ×4 means order 0, 1 or 2.
Never take orders from equation coefficients; use only the data.
Overall order = sum of all the exponents.
if_lost: Which two experiments keep [NO] the same?
By what factor does [O2] change between them?
By what factor does the rate change in that same pair?
Now find a pair where only [NO] changes.

1_context.short: AO3: deduce the orders from experimental data.
1_context.why: R2.2.9 says rate equations can only be found by experiment. This tests reading the data, not the balanced equation.
1_context.avoid: Copying the coefficients 2 and 1 as orders: they happen to match here, but that is not a method.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.9: rate equations depend on the mechanism and can only be determined experimentally.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use exact doublings. Exams use rounded rates (0.057, 0.227), so the factors come out near 2 and near 4.

2_markscheme_logic.short: The correct rate expression alone earns both marks.
2_markscheme_logic.why: M1 is both orders and M2 is the expression. The markscheme gives [2] for a correct expression, because it already shows the orders.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Giving orders with no supporting ratio: the 07M.2.HL.TZ0.1 report notes marks lost for missing reasons.
trigger_phrases: first order with respect to O2 AND second order with respect to NO
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: M1 needs both orders correct. M2 needs k and the correct exponents.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: orders only, or k left out. Full: rate = k[NO]^2[O2].

3_novel_application.short: Rates 0.057 and 0.227 are rounded: read them as ×2 and ×4.
3_novel_application.why: 0.057/0.028 ≈ 2.04 and 0.227/0.057 ≈ 3.98. Real data are never exact, and only integer orders are assessed.
3_novel_application.disguise: Rounded rates, and a table where the obvious pair is not adjacent.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Round each rate ratio to the nearest of 1, 2, 4 or 8.

4_command_terms.short: Determine: show the ratio used for each reactant.
4_command_terms.why: Shown ratios secure M1 and allow error carried forward into later parts, such as calculating k.
4_command_terms.avoid: A bare answer: the 02M.2.HL.TZ0.1 report advises showing how each order was deduced.
4_command_terms.demands: The order for each reactant, plus a complete rate expression including k.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 2 marks: both orders, then the rate expression. A correct expression scores [2].

5_time_efficiency.short: Two ratios, then write the expression.
5_time_efficiency.why: Exp 1 and Exp 3 differ in both concentrations, so that pair needs extra algebra and wastes time.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Don't calculate k unless asked, and skip the Exp 1–3 pair.

6_data_booklet.short: The booklet has nothing on this; it is pure ratio work.
6_data_booklet.why: Rate equations and order rules are not in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the booklet for rate equations.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Doubling a concentration multiplies the rate by 1, 2 or 4 for orders 0, 1 or 2.

7_elimination.short: Any answer that is non-integer or has no k is out.
7_elimination.why: Integer orders and an explicit k are fixed requirements, so these answers fail with no calculation.

definitely_wrong.rule: Only integer orders are assessed.

definitely_wrong.target: A rate expression with no k
definitely_wrong.rule: Not a rate expression; leaving out k was flagged (02M.2.HL.TZ0.1).

definitely_wrong.target: An equilibrium-style expression with products in it
definitely_wrong.rule: Products never appear in a rate expression (09N.2.HL.TZ0.6).

walkthrough.answer: First order in O2: from Exp 1 to 2, [O2] doubles and the rate doubles. Second order in NO: from Exp 2 to 3, [NO] doubles and the rate rises about four times. Rate = k[NO]^2[O2].

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.9–R2.2.10: deduce the rate equation from data; order is the exponent; overall order is the sum.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach clean doublings. Exams add a catalyst column, give reaction times instead of rates, or ask for the overall order.

trigger_phrases: order with respect to each named reactant
trap_boundaries: Writing a rate expression in the form of an equilibrium expression is wrong (09N.2.HL.TZ0.6).
The overall order is the sum of exponents: 21% chose second instead of third (25M.1A.HL.6213.27).
[A] with no power means first order, not zero order (02M.2.HL.TZ0.1).
Give an order for every species in the table, not just those in the equation (10M.2.HL.TZ1.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: the orders. Full: orders plus a correct rate expression that includes k.

disguises: A catalyst such as H+ appears in the table and has its own order (25M.1A.HL.6207.30).
Times are given instead of rates: rate ∝ 1/time, so halving a concentration doubles the time for first order (07M.1.HL.TZ0.20; 14M.2.HL.TZ2.6).
The question asks only for the overall order (25M.1A.HL.6213.27).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Find a pair where only one concentration changes. If there is none, use an order you already know to cancel its effect.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Usually one mark for the orders and one for the expression. Wrong orders carry forward (ECF) into k.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip calculating k unless the question asks for it.

6_data_booklet.hack: Rate equations and the rules for reading orders are NOT in the booklet: memorise them.

rules: Only integer orders (0, 1, 2) are assessed.
If the rate is unchanged when a concentration changes, that species is zero order.
If halving a concentration quarters the rate, that species is second order.

evidence.note: Part (a)(ii): three-run table for 2NO + O2.
First order in O2, second order in NO; rate = k[NO]^2[O2]; [2] for the correct expression.
Mean 1.55/2; almost all deduced both orders.
Overall order is third (D).
66% correct; 21% chose second order.
Orders 1, 0, 1 including the catalyst H+ (A).
Marks lost when no reason was given for an order.
k omitted, and [A] with no power misread as zero order.
Orders deduced for only some of the substances.

cards.difficulty_signal: Usually well prepared (1.55/2 on 24N.2.HL.TZ0.6), but 21% got the wrong overall order in 25M.1A.HL.6213.27. 'Solving problems in order of reactions' was flagged difficult in May 2025.

cards.title: Units of k come from the overall order, not from the number of species

walkthrough.question:
A reaction has the rate equation rate = k[X]^2[Y]^0. What are the units of k?
A. mol2 dm−6 s−1
B. mol dm−3 s−1
C. mol−1 dm3 s−1
D. mol−2 dm6 s−1
walkthrough.key_idea: Units of k = (mol dm−3)^(1−n) s−1, where n is the overall order.
walkthrough.question_type: Units of the rate constant k
walkthrough.careful: A zero-order term adds nothing: the overall order here is 2.
procedure: Add the exponents to get the overall order n.
Rearrange: k = rate ÷ [concentration]^n.
Substitute units: mol dm−3 s−1 ÷ (mol dm−3)^n.
Cancel, then write the leftover terms with negative powers.
tricks: Orders 0, 1, 2, 3 give mol dm−3 s−1; s−1; mol−1 dm3 s−1; mol−2 dm6 s−1.
The powers of mol and dm always have opposite signs; dm's power is −3 times mol's.
if_lost: What is the overall order of this rate equation?
What does a term raised to the power 0 contribute?
Rearrange the rate equation to make k the subject.

1_context.short: AO2: work out units from the overall order.
1_context.why: R2.2.11 says k's units depend on the overall order. The question tests whether you can do that unit algebra.
1_context.avoid: Treating [Y]^0 as if Y were first order.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.11: k depends on temperature, and its units are determined by the overall order.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give a table of units. Exams make you work them out, often with a zero-order term shown.

2_markscheme_logic.why: Rate is always mol dm−3 s−1. Dividing by (mol dm−3)^2 leaves one mol dm−3 on the bottom, which gives mol−1 dm3 s−1.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Guessing from memory: fewer than 43% were right (25M.1A.HL.6219.28 report).
trigger_phrases: mol−1 dm3 s−1 for overall second order
mol−2 dm6 s−1 for overall third order (24N.2.HL.TZ0.6)
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: In written questions, wrong or missing units lose the units mark (08M.2.HL.TZ0.7).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: C versus D: D is for third order. C correctly gives the zero-order term no units.

3_novel_application.short: The [Y]^0 term tempts you to count Y.
3_novel_application.why: Anything raised to the power 0 equals 1 and has no units, so Y does not enter the overall order.
3_novel_application.avoid: Counting the species in the rate equation instead of adding the exponents.
3_novel_application.disguise: A zero-order term is written in explicitly as a distractor.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Overall order = sum of exponents; a zero counts as zero.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: work the units out instead of recalling them.
4_command_terms.why: None of the distractors stood out, so students were guessing (25M.1A.HL.6219.28). Working it out removes the guess.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose k's units for an overall order of 2.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 1 mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Overall order 2 gives mol−1 dm3 s−1.
5_time_efficiency.why: Once the order-to-units pattern is learnt, this takes seconds.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing out the full division when the pattern is already known.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No dimensional working needed once the 0–3 pattern is known.

6_data_booklet.short: Units of k are not in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.why: The booklet lists equations and constants, not rate-constant units.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the booklet for units of k.
6_data_booklet.memorise: k units = mol^(1−n) dm^(3n−3) s−1 for overall order n.

7_elimination.short: Rule out A, B and D without any algebra.
7_elimination.why: Each wrong option matches a different order (−1, 0 or 3), never 2.
7_elimination.avoid: Picking D because X is squared.

definitely_wrong.rule: A positive power of mol would need overall order −1, which is impossible.
mol dm−3 s−1 is the unit of rate, so it fits only a zero-order k.
mol−2 dm6 s−1 needs an overall order of 3.

walkthrough.answer: C. The overall order is 2, so k = (mol dm−3 s−1) ÷ (mol dm−3)^2 = mol−1 dm3 s−1.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.11: solve rate-equation problems, including the units of k.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show a table of units. Exams ask for k's value and units together after a rate-data question.

trigger_phrases: units worked out from the overall order
mol−2 dm6 s−1 for third order (24N.2.HL.TZ0.6)
trap_boundaries: Many lose the mark for wrong or missing units of k (08M.2.HL.TZ0.7; 04N.2.HL.TZ0.8).
If times are in minutes the unit is min−1, not s−1 (05N.2.HL.TZ0.1).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: The value alone earns partial credit; the value with correct units earns full credit.

disguises: A zero-order term written into the rate equation (25M.1A.HL.6219.28).
Time measured in minutes or hours (05N.2.HL.TZ0.1).
k asked for straight after a rate-data table (24N.2.HL.TZ0.6).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Overall order → 1 − n → s−1, or whatever time unit the question uses.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: In written questions the value and the units are usually separate marks (24N.2.HL.TZ0.6: 7.1 × 10^3, then mol−2 dm6 s−1).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the dimensional algebra once the 0–3 pattern is memorised.

6_data_booklet.hack: Units of k are NOT in the booklet; memorise the pattern.

rules: For order 1 or more, k never has a positive power of mol.
mol dm−3 s−1 is the unit of k only for zero order.
s−1 on its own means first order.

evidence.note: rate = k[X]^2[Y]^0; answer C, mol−1 dm3 s−1.
Under 43% correct; no distractor was particularly attractive.
k = 7.1 × 10^3 with units mol−2 dm6 s−1, as a separate mark.
Units of the rate constant often wrong.
Many could not give the correct units.
Missed that time was in minutes, not seconds.

cards.difficulty_signal: Under 43% correct on 25M.1A.HL.6219.28. 'Rate constant' is the second most frequent examiner error phrase (n=10), and unit errors recur from 2004 to 2024.

cards.title: Rate equation from a mechanism: slow step, then replace the intermediate

walkthrough.question:
An exothermic reaction between A and B happens in two steps:
Step 1 (fast): A + B → C + D
Step 2 (slow): D + B → E
Deduce the rate equation for the reaction. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: The slow step sets the rate; replace intermediate D with what forms it.
walkthrough.careful: Replace the intermediate with the reactants of the fast step.
procedure: Find the slow (rate-determining) step.
Write rate = k[reactants of that step].
Find intermediates: made in one step, used in a later one.
Replace each intermediate with the reactants that formed it.
Add the powers of any species that appears twice.
tricks: If the slow step is first, the rate equation is just its reactants.
Species that react only after the slow step never appear.
Check: the exponents add up to the reactant particles used up to the end of the slow step.
if_lost: Which step is slow?
Is every species in the slow step one of the starting reactants?
Which step produces D?

1_context.short: AO3: rate law when the slow step comes second.
1_context.why: R2.2.6 guidance asks for examples where the rate-determining step is not the first step. That case is exactly what is tested here.
1_context.avoid: Writing rate = k[D][B]: D is an intermediate.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.6: the slowest step determines the rate; mechanisms must be consistent with kinetic data.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books mostly show mechanisms whose slow step is first. Exams put the slow step second, so you must replace the intermediate.

2_markscheme_logic.short: A is first order, B second order: rate = k[A][B]^2.
2_markscheme_logic.why: M1 is both orders and M2 is the full equation. A correct equation on its own scores [2].
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Stopping at the slow step's species; this part drew comment from teachers (25M.2.HL.6221.8 report) and was flagged difficult in May 2025.
trigger_phrases: A: first order AND B: second order
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: A rate equation that contains an intermediate (D) or a product scores nothing.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: k[A][B] counts B only once. k[A][B]^2 counts B in both steps.

3_novel_application.short: Letters, not real formulas, hide which species is the intermediate.
3_novel_application.why: D is made in step 1 and used in step 2, so it is the intermediate. C and E are never used again, so they are the products (part (a)(i)).
3_novel_application.avoid: Putting C into the rate equation.
3_novel_application.disguise: Abstract letters A–E with no chemistry to lean on.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Made, then used = intermediate, so it never appears in the rate equation.

4_command_terms.short: Deduce: reason from the steps to the rate equation.
4_command_terms.why: Deduce means reaching a conclusion from the information given: the steps and which one is slow.
4_command_terms.avoid: Guessing orders from the overall equation.
4_command_terms.demands: The rate equation, with the orders that follow from the mechanism.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 2 marks: the orders, then the equation. A correct equation earns both.

5_time_efficiency.short: Slow step, swap D, add the powers of B.
5_time_efficiency.why: Three moves give the answer. No equilibrium algebra is needed at IB level.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Deriving an equilibrium constant for the fast step.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip any working with K for the fast step.

6_data_booklet.short: The booklet has nothing on mechanisms.
6_data_booklet.why: Rate-determining-step rules are not in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for rate equations in section 1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The slowest step sets the rate. Intermediates are replaced by the reactants that formed them.

7_elimination.short: Any rate equation containing D, C or E is wrong.
7_elimination.why: Intermediates and products never appear in a rate equation built from the starting reactants.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping D because it appears in the slow step.

definitely_wrong.rule: D is an intermediate.

definitely_wrong.target: A rate equation containing C or E
definitely_wrong.rule: Products never appear in the rate equation.
A forms D, which feeds the slow step.

walkthrough.answer: rate = k[A][B]^2. The slow step uses D and B, and D comes from A + B in the fast step, so the reaction is first order in A and second order in B.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.6 and R2.2.9: the rate-determining step; the rate equation depends on the mechanism.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show slow-first examples. Exams use a fast step before the slow one, or ask you to judge whether a mechanism fits a given rate equation.

trigger_phrases: rate = k[...] matching what feeds the slow step
trap_boundaries: A product or an intermediate in the rate equation is wrong.
The steps must add up to the overall stoichiometric equation (04M.2.HL.TZ0.1).
The rate-determining step must balance in both atoms and charge (14M.2.HL.TZ1.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: the slow step's species copied, intermediate included. Full: the intermediate replaced by its source reactants.

disguises: Slow step second, after a fast step (25M.2.HL.6221.8; 25N.1A.HL.6219.26).
Slow step first, so a later reactant such as CO drops out of the rate equation (24N.1.HL.TZ0.21).
Asked whether a mechanism agrees with a given rate expression (04M.2.HL.TZ0.1).
3_novel_application.heuristic: The rate equation contains every starting reactant used up to and including the slow step, but no intermediates.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Usually 1–2 marks. Evaluate items reward agreement with the kinetic data and with the stoichiometry as separate points (04M.2.HL.TZ0.1).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No equilibrium-constant algebra is needed.

6_data_booklet.hack: Mechanism rules and rate equations are NOT in the booklet.

rules: Species that react only in steps after the slow step are zero order.
Intermediates and products never appear in the rate equation.
A species that appears in both the fast and the slow step has its powers added.

evidence.note: Two-step mechanism with the slow step second; part (a)(iii) asks for the rate equation.
A first order, B second order; rate = k[A][B]^2; [2] for the correct equation.
Teachers commented on deducing the rate equation from this mechanism.
Fast step then slow step; rate = k[Br2][NO]^2 (B).
Slow step first; rate = k[NO2]^2 (A).
About 75% deduced the rate equation correctly.
Weaker students did not see the intermediate X depends on H2 and NO; the mechanism must match the stoichiometry.
Few wrote a balanced equation for the rate-determining step.

cards.difficulty_signal: Examiner findings flag 'deducing the rate equation from a mechanism' as difficult in May 2025, May 2019, May 2014, Nov 2014 and Nov 2012. About 75% succeed when the slow step is first.

cards.title: Multistep energy profile: one peak per step, and the slow step's peak has the larger Ea

walkthrough.question:
The same exothermic reaction goes by two steps:
Step 1 (fast): A + B → C + D
Step 2 (slow): D + B → E
Sketch the energy profile (potential energy against reaction coordinate). Label the reactants, products, transition state(s) and intermediate(s). [3]
walkthrough.key_idea: Two peaks; the slow step's peak has the larger Ea.
walkthrough.question_type: Sketch energy profile for multistep reaction
walkthrough.careful: Make the slow step's activation energy the larger of the two.
procedure: Draw one hump for each elementary step.
Put products below reactants if the reaction is exothermic.
Put the intermediate in the dip between the humps.
Make the slow step's Ea, measured from its own start, larger.
Label reactants, products, each transition state and the intermediate.
tricks: Peaks are transition states; dips are intermediates.
Measure each Ea from the energy level just before its own peak.
if_lost: How many elementary steps are there, so how many peaks?
Which step is slow, and what does slow mean for its barrier?
Where on the curve do C + D sit?

1_context.short: AO2: build an energy profile from a mechanism.
1_context.why: R2.2.7 says energy profiles show the activation energy and transition state of the rate-determining step. Here you have to construct one yourself.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.7: energy profiles show the Ea and transition state of the rate-determining step in a multistep reaction.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books mostly draw one-hump profiles. This question needs two humps, sized according to which step is slow.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Two transition states; larger second Ea with lower products; all labels.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The third mark needs the slow step's barrier to be bigger. Only a small proportion of stronger students did this (25M.2.HL.6221.8 report).
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Drawing two equal humps, or a bigger first hump.
trigger_phrases: Ea of second step is larger AND products lower than reactants
labels for reactants, products, both transition states and the intermediate
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: An intermediate drawn above the reactants is not penalised. Ea and ΔH labels are not required.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: 2/3 becomes 3/3 when the second hump's Ea, measured from the intermediate, is larger than the first.

3_novel_application.short: No energies are given; 'fast' and 'slow' are the only data.
3_novel_application.why: A slow step has a higher barrier, so the speeds tell you which hump to draw taller.
3_novel_application.avoid: Guessing the hump sizes, or making both the same.
3_novel_application.disguise: Letters only, no numbers: the step speeds stand in for barrier heights.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Slow means high barrier. The number of steps is the number of peaks.

4_command_terms.short: Sketch: the right shape and labels, not to scale.
4_command_terms.why: A sketch gives the general shape and relevant features. The marks are for the features, not for accuracy.
4_command_terms.avoid: Spending time on scale or exact energies.
4_command_terms.demands: A labelled profile showing two steps, the intermediate and an exothermic overall change.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 3 marks, one per feature group (per point).

5_time_efficiency.short: Two humps, slow one taller, products lower, label everything.
5_time_efficiency.why: Each mark is a single visual feature, so draw those features and stop.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the ΔH and Ea arrows here: they are not required.

6_data_booklet.why: Profile conventions are not in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Transition states are maxima and intermediates are minima. The slow step has the largest barrier.

7_elimination.short: Single humps, endothermic shapes and MB curves fail.
7_elimination.why: Each one contradicts a fact given in the stem or the type of graph asked for.

definitely_wrong.rule: Two elementary steps need two transition states.
The reaction is exothermic.
Wrong type of graph; it scored nothing (24N.2.SL.TZ0.3 report).

walkthrough.answer: Two humps with both transition states labelled. The intermediate (C + D) sits in the dip between them. The second hump is taller, with a larger Ea measured from the intermediate. The products (C + E) end below the reactants (A + B).

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.6–R2.2.7: tell intermediates from transition states and recognise both on energy profiles.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books label a single transition state. Exams want intermediates as dips, and the rate-determining step's barrier as the largest.

trigger_phrases: Ea of the slow step larger
trap_boundaries: Intermediate at an energy minimum; its height relative to reactants is ignored (25M.2.HL.6209.6; 25M.2.HL.6221.8).
Axes must be reaction progress/coordinate and potential energy; 'time' alone is not accepted (24N.2.HL.TZ0.4).
Ea is an upward or double-headed arrow, never a downward one (24N.2.HL.TZ0.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Two peaks earn the first mark. Correct labels earn the second. The larger slow-step barrier earns the third.

disguises: Abstract letters with 'fast' and 'slow' as the only clues (25M.2.HL.6221.8).
A colour-change reaction whose first step forms an unstable complex (25M.2.HL.6209.6).
A profile asked for straight after a Maxwell–Boltzmann part (24N.2.SL.TZ0.3).
3_novel_application.heuristic: The number of steps is the number of peaks; the slow step has the tallest barrier from its own start.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Marks are given per feature (per point), for example 3–4 marks: shape, exothermic level, Ea of each step, ΔH (25M.2.HL.6209.6).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No scale, no numbers.

6_data_booklet.hack: Profile conventions are NOT in the booklet.

rules: A two-step mechanism never has a single-peak profile.
An exothermic profile always ends lower than it starts.
An intermediate is never drawn at a peak.

evidence.note: Part (a)(ii): sketch the profile of a two-step exothermic reaction.
Two transition states; larger second-step Ea and lower products; correct labels. An intermediate above the reactants is not penalised.
Most showed two peaks, about half labelled correctly, and only stronger students showed the larger second Ea.
Intermediate at an energy minimum; Ea of both steps; ΔH from reactants down to products.
Axis labels required; a downward Ea arrow is not accepted.
Some drew a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve instead of an energy profile and scored nothing.

cards.difficulty_signal: Only a small proportion of students earned the third mark on 25M.2.HL.6221.8(a)(ii). The paper 24N.2.SL.TZ0.3 (one of the hardest, 20%) showed profile and axis errors.

cards.title: Single-step energy profile: exothermic means the reverse Ea is larger

walkthrough.question:
Methane burns: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l), ΔH = −891 kJ. Which row gives the relative bond strengths and the relative activation energies?
A. Product bonds weaker than reactant bonds; Ea forward > Ea reverse
B. Product bonds stronger than reactant bonds; Ea forward < Ea reverse
C. Product bonds stronger than reactant bonds; Ea forward > Ea reverse
D. Product bonds weaker than reactant bonds; Ea forward < Ea reverse
walkthrough.key_idea: Exothermic: stronger bonds in the products, and reverse Ea = forward Ea + |ΔH|.
walkthrough.question_type: Energy profile: Ea forward vs reverse
walkthrough.careful: Measure the reverse Ea from the products' level up to the peak.
procedure: Read the sign of ΔH.
Sketch reactants, the peak and products at the right heights.
Forward Ea: from reactants up to the peak.
Reverse Ea: from products up to the peak.
Exothermic: bonds formed are stronger than bonds broken.
tricks: Ea(reverse) − Ea(forward) = −ΔH.
ΔH < 0 gives stronger product bonds and a larger reverse barrier.
if_lost: Is this reaction exothermic or endothermic?
On the profile, which is lower: reactants or products?
From which level is the reverse barrier measured?

1_context.short: AO2: read Ea and bond strength from the sign of ΔH.
1_context.why: R2.2.5 asks you to sketch and explain energy profiles. Reading the reverse barrier off a profile is the applied skill.
1_context.avoid: Thinking the forward and reverse barriers are the same height.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.4–R2.2.5: Ea is a minimum energy; sketch energy profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books mark the forward Ea only. Exams ask about the reverse barrier and link it to bond strength.

2_markscheme_logic.short: B: stronger product bonds; forward Ea smaller than reverse.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Products sit 891 kJ lower, so climbing back to the same peak from the products is longer than from the reactants.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Thinking 'stronger bonds are harder to break, so the forward Ea is bigger' (option C).
trigger_phrases: products lower in energy than reactants
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Both halves must be right: the bond-strength half and the Ea half.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B versus C: C has the right bonds but measures the reverse barrier wrongly.

3_novel_application.short: A combustion question that is really about profile geometry.
3_novel_application.why: Every fact needed follows from the sign of ΔH; no bond enthalpy values are needed.
3_novel_application.avoid: Trying to calculate the bond enthalpies.
3_novel_application.disguise: A bond-strength wording sits on top of a kinetics question.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Sketch the profile: lower products mean stronger bonds and a taller reverse climb.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: check each half of the row separately.
4_command_terms.why: Two-part rows double the traps; settle one column first, then the other.
4_command_terms.avoid: Judging the whole row at a glance.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the row that is correct for both bond strength and Ea.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 1 mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.why: One sign decides the bond strengths and which barrier is bigger.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip bond enthalpy values entirely.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet section is needed; ΔH is given.
6_data_booklet.why: The relationship between the two barriers is geometric, so no data are required.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH. This is NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Weaker product bonds contradict ΔH < 0: A and D are out.
7_elimination.why: Releasing energy means the bonds formed are stronger than the bonds broken.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping D for its correct Ea half.

definitely_wrong.rule: Weaker product bonds would make the reaction endothermic.
Weaker product bonds contradict ΔH < 0.
For an exothermic reaction the forward Ea cannot exceed the reverse Ea.

walkthrough.answer: B. The reaction is exothermic, so the products are lower in energy and have stronger bonds. The reverse barrier is therefore larger than the forward one.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.5: sketch and explain energy profiles with and without catalysts for endothermic and exothermic reactions.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books draw a single labelled hump. Exams test the axis labels, the direction of the Ea arrow and the reverse barrier.

trigger_phrases: labelled Ea from reactants to the peak
trap_boundaries: 'Time' alone on the x-axis is not accepted (24N.2.HL.TZ0.4).
A downward Ea arrow is not accepted; a double-headed arrow is (24N.2.HL.TZ0.4).
Symmetric curves and swapped catalysed and uncatalysed Ea values are common errors (11N.2.HL.TZ0.8).
Missing Ea or missing labels lose marks (04N.2.SL.TZ0.3; 09M.2.SL.TZ2.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: the curve shape only. Full: labelled axes, correct levels, and an Ea arrow going up from the reactants.

disguises: Bond-strength wording on a profile question (20N.1.HL.TZ0.15).
An endothermic reaction shown instead of an exothermic one (09M.2.SL.TZ2.4).
Catalysed and uncatalysed curves drawn on the same axes (11N.2.HL.TZ0.8).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Draw it: products below reactants means exothermic, stronger bonds and a bigger reverse barrier.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Usually 3 marks: axes (1), exothermic or endothermic curve (1), labelled Ea (1) (24N.2.HL.TZ0.4).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No numbers on the axes unless they are given.

6_data_booklet.hack: Energy-profile conventions and the Ea(reverse) relationship are NOT in the booklet.

rules: For an exothermic reaction, Ea(forward) < Ea(reverse).
For an endothermic reaction, Ea(forward) > ΔH.
A catalyst lowers both barriers by the same amount and leaves ΔH unchanged.

evidence.note: Exothermic methane combustion: stronger product bonds, forward Ea < reverse.
Answer B.
Axes must be reaction progress and potential energy; a downward Ea arrow is not accepted.
Wrong axis labels, symmetric curves, catalysed and uncatalysed Ea mixed up.
Labels missing; some drew an endothermic profile instead.
Some failed to show the activation energy.

cards.difficulty_signal: Annotating profiles with Ea was well prepared in Nov 2024, but axis and arrow errors recur in reports from 2004 to 2024.

cards.title: Catalysts: a new mechanism with lower Ea; particles gain no energy; the catalyst is not used up

walkthrough.question:
Pick the one true statement about how a catalyst works.
A. They raise the kinetic energy of the reacting particles.
B. They speed up endothermic reactions more than exothermic ones.
C. They speed up a reaction and are used up in it.
D. They change the mechanism of a reaction.
walkthrough.key_idea: A catalyst gives a new pathway (mechanism) with lower Ea and is not used up.
walkthrough.careful: A catalyst lowers Ea; it never changes the particles' energies.
procedure: Recall: a catalyst gives an alternative pathway with lower Ea.
A catalyst is regenerated at the end, not consumed.
The MB curve stays the same; the Ea line moves to lower energy.
Forward and reverse reactions speed up equally; K is unchanged.
Test each statement against these facts.
tricks: A statement giving particles more energy describes temperature, not a catalyst.
'Alternative pathway' and 'different mechanism' mean the same thing.
if_lost: Does a catalyst change the particles, or the route they take?
Is the catalyst still there at the end?
Which statement really describes heating?

1_context.short: AO1: what a catalyst changes and what it doesn't.
1_context.why: R2.2.5 says catalysts provide an alternative pathway with lower Ea. Exam distractors swap in effects that belong to temperature.
1_context.avoid: Mixing up the effect of a catalyst with the effect of temperature.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.5: catalysts increase rate by providing an alternative pathway with lower Ea.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books say 'lowers Ea'. Exams use the equivalent wording 'alters the mechanism'.

2_markscheme_logic.short: D: a catalyst provides a new mechanism (pathway).
2_markscheme_logic.why: A new pathway is a new set of elementary steps, which is a different mechanism with a lower barrier.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Option A: 'catalyst increases kinetic energy' is a common mistake (19M.2.SL.TZ2.2 report).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: M1 needs a pathway from reactants to products, not only 'different route' wording (25M.2.HL.6209.6).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: D versus A: a catalyst changes the route, not the energy the particles have.

3_novel_application.why: The examiner rewords the definition, so you have to recognise that the two phrases mean the same.
3_novel_application.avoid: Rejecting D because it isn't the textbook phrase.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Translate each option into the textbook statement before judging it.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: find the one true statement.
4_command_terms.why: Each distractor is a known misconception, so each can be ruled out by one fact.
4_command_terms.avoid: Choosing the option that sounds most energetic.
4_command_terms.demands: Pick the correct statement about how catalysts work.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 1 mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Ask: does it change particles, the route, or get used up?
5_time_efficiency.why: Three checks clear all three distractors.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Ignore the endothermic and exothermic wording: catalysts lower both barriers.

6_data_booklet.short: Catalyst facts are not in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.why: The booklet has no kinetics theory.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Alternative pathway, lower Ea, regenerated, K unchanged, MB curve unchanged.

7_elimination.short: A, B and C each break one catalyst fact.
7_elimination.why: Each distractor is a textbook misconception that one fact disproves.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping C because catalysts do take part in steps.

definitely_wrong.rule: Only temperature raises particle kinetic energy.
A catalyst lowers the barrier for any reaction; the type of ΔH doesn't matter.
A catalyst is regenerated, not used up.

walkthrough.answer: D. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway, which is a different mechanism with a lower Ea.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.5: catalysts and lower Ea; Maxwell–Boltzmann curves showing different Ea values.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books state the definition. Exams want it linked to the MB curve (more particles with E ≥ Ea) and to equilibrium (K unchanged).

trap_boundaries: M1 needs a description of a route from reactants to products if the exact wording is missing (25M.2.HL.6209.6).
Explain the increase using more particles with E ≥ Ea, not more frequent collisions (12M.2.SL.TZ2.1; 19M.2.HL.TZ2.2).
A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally and does not change Kc (06M.2.SL.TZ0.6; 08M.2.SL.TZ0.7).
Say the catalyst is unchanged or regenerated (25M.2.SL.TZ2.3; 11N.2.HL.TZ0.8).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: 'lowers Ea'. Full: alternative pathway with lower Ea, so a larger fraction of collisions have E ≥ Ea.

disguises: 'Alters the mechanism' wording (25N.1A.HL.6219.27).
A volume–time graph: the catalysed curve is steeper but ends at the same final volume (24N.1.HL.TZ0.19).
A species regenerated in a mechanism, such as NO, is the catalyst (11N.2.HL.TZ0.8).
Which change lowers Ea: a catalyst, not a higher temperature (08N.1.SL.TZ0.20).
3_novel_application.heuristic: A catalyst moves the Ea line; temperature changes the curve. The amount of product never changes.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Explain items are typically 2 marks: alternative pathway (1), lower Ea (1) (25M.2.HL.6209.6).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: The details of homogeneous and heterogeneous catalyst mechanisms are not assessed.

6_data_booklet.hack: Catalyst theory is NOT in the booklet.

rules: A catalyst never changes ΔH, K or the final amount of product.
A catalyst never raises particle kinetic energy.
On an MB plot, a catalyst leaves the curve the same and moves Ea to the left.

evidence.note: Correct statement: catalysts alter the mechanism (D).
Alternative pathway (M1, needs a reactants-to-products description) and lower Ea (M2).
A common mistake was saying molecules gain kinetic energy when a catalyst is added.
Students rarely explained that more molecules have energy ≥ Ea.
A catalyst does not change Kc or the position of equilibrium.
Ea is changed by a catalyst, not by temperature; 61% correct.
Catalysed gas-volume curve: answer B; 90% correct.
Many missed that the solid catalyst is unchanged.

cards.difficulty_signal: Catalyst action was well prepared in Nov 2024 and Nov 2014, but 'the way a catalyst works' was flagged difficult in May 2019, and 'catalyst raises KE' recurs as an error.

cards.title: Arrhenius plot: ln k against 1/T has gradient −Ea/R; convert J to kJ

walkthrough.question:
Rate constants measured at several temperatures were plotted as ln k against 1/T, giving a straight line. The linear Arrhenius equation is ln k = −Ea/(RT) + ln A. What does the gradient of the line equal?
A. −Ea/R
B. −Ea
C. ln A
D. −Ea/RT
walkthrough.key_idea: ln k against 1/T has gradient −Ea/R and intercept ln A.
walkthrough.careful: Ea = −gradient × R gives J mol−1; divide by 1000 for kJ.
procedure: Match ln k = (−Ea/R)(1/T) + ln A to y = mx + c.
y is ln k; x is 1/T.
Gradient m = −Ea/R; intercept c = ln A.
To find Ea: Ea = −m × 8.31, in J mol−1.
Convert to kJ mol−1 if the question asks.
tricks: The gradient is always negative; Ea is always positive.
The gradient has units of K, and K × R gives J mol−1.
if_lost: What is plotted on the x-axis?
Rewrite the booklet equation in the form y = mx + c.
What multiplies 1/T in that equation?

1_context.short: AO2: match the linear Arrhenius form to y = mx + c.
1_context.why: R2.2.12 asks you to analyse the linear form of the Arrhenius equation. The booklet gives the equation; you have to read the gradient from it.
1_context.avoid: Memorising 'gradient = Ea' without the minus sign and R.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.12: the Arrhenius equation and its linear form are used to find Ea from graphs.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books derive the linear form. Exams give a numerical gradient and ask for Ea with R and a kJ conversion.

2_markscheme_logic.why: x is 1/T, so T is already part of the x variable. Only −Ea/R multiplies x.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Option D, which keeps T inside the gradient; about 22% missed this (24N.1.HL.TZ0.20 report: 78% correct).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Written items accept the gradient within a range (1.4–1.5 × 10^3 K in 25M.2.HL.6215.3); it must be negative.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A versus D: whether you saw that 1/T is the x variable, not a constant.

3_novel_application.short: The equation looks complicated, but it is just a straight line.
3_novel_application.why: Whatever multiplies x is the gradient; whatever stands alone is the intercept.
3_novel_application.avoid: Treating the R and T together as one constant.
3_novel_application.disguise: A numerical gradient, such as −6400, with options already in kJ (25M.1A.HL.6207.31).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Whatever is in front of x is the gradient.

4_command_terms.why: A one-step recognition of the gradient, but the distractors are close.
4_command_terms.avoid: Picking the option with the most symbols.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose what the gradient of ln k against 1/T represents.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 1 mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Write y = mx + c beside the equation and read off m.
5_time_efficiency.why: Lining up the terms takes seconds and removes the ambiguity.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Deriving the equation from k = Ae^(−Ea/RT).
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No need to take logs yourself: the linear form is in the booklet.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 1 gives both Arrhenius forms; section 2 gives R.
6_data_booklet.why: The booklet gives the equations and R = 8.31 J K−1 mol−1, so only the matching to y = mx + c is left.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Using R = 8.31 and forgetting the result is in J, not kJ.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 1: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) and ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A. Section 2: R = 8.31 J K−1 mol−1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Gradient = −Ea/R and intercept = ln A; the booklet does not state these.

7_elimination.short: B, C and D fail on units or role.
7_elimination.why: The gradient of ln k against 1/T has units of K, which only −Ea/R gives.
7_elimination.avoid: Picking C because ln A is in the equation.

definitely_wrong.rule: No R: the units cannot match a gradient measured in K.
ln A is the y-intercept, not the gradient.
It contains T, but T is on the x-axis, not a constant.

walkthrough.answer: A. The gradient equals −Ea/R; the y-intercept is ln A.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.12–R2.2.13: k depends on temperature; find Ea and A from experimental data.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books stop at the equation. Exams ask for the axes, the gradient, Ea with units, and the qualitative link between T and k.

trap_boundaries: Factor-of-10 or factor-of-100 errors from axis multipliers (11M.2.HL.TZ1.2; 13M.2.HL.TZ1.3).
Wrong gradient or wrong units, J versus kJ, lose the Ea mark (13M.2.HL.TZ2.2; 11M.2.HL.TZ1.2).
Describing the relationship between k and T as linear is wrong (13M.2.HL.TZ2.2).
Vague 'use the gradient and R' descriptions don't earn the method marks (14M.2.HL.TZ1.2; 18M.2.HL.TZ1.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: gradient read correctly. Full: Ea = −gradient × R with the correct sign, power of ten and units.

disguises: Gradient given as −6400 with options in kJ (25M.1A.HL.6207.31).
Asked to state only the axes needed (25M.2.HL.6215.3).
Axis scaled as 1/T × 10^−3 (13M.2.HL.TZ1.3).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Line up the equation with y = mx + c, then check units: K × J K−1 mol−1 gives J mol−1.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Written items give separate marks: axes 1/T and ln k (1), gradient (1), Ea with units (1) (25M.2.HL.6215.3).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Don't rederive the linear form; it is printed in section 1.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 1 has k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) and ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A. Section 2 has R = 8.31 J K−1 mol−1. That the gradient is −Ea/R is NOT stated: read it off.

rules: The gradient of ln k against 1/T is always negative for Ea > 0.
Any expression for the gradient that contains T is wrong.
Ea from R = 8.31 comes out in J mol−1, not kJ mol−1.

evidence.note: Gradient of ln k against 1/T is −Ea/R (A).
About 78% knew the gradient is −Ea/R.
Axes 1/T and ln k; gradient −1444 K accepted within 1.4–1.5 × 10^3.
Slope −6400 converted to Ea in kJ mol−1 using R (B).
Answers out by a factor of 100; units ignored.
10^−2 omitted when finding Ea graphically.
The T–k relationship described as linear; wrong gradient or units.
Explanations of how to find Ea were vague.
Most could not describe how to determine Ea.

cards.difficulty_signal: 78% on the gradient MCQ, but graphical Ea determination was flagged difficult in Nov 2011, Nov 2012 and May 2018. 'Activation energy' is the top examiner error phrase (n=17).

cards.title: Molecularity counts the particles in one elementary step (SN2 is bimolecular)

walkthrough.question:
Which statement about the SN2 mechanism is correct?
A. Two particles take part in the rate-determining step.
B. The mechanism has two steps.
C. An electrophile replaces a nucleophile.
D. A carbocation intermediate forms.
walkthrough.key_idea: SN2 is one bimolecular step: the nucleophile and substrate collide.
walkthrough.careful: Molecularity counts particles in one step; order comes from experiment.
procedure: Write out the rate-determining elementary step.
Count the reacting particles on its left side.
1 = unimolecular, 2 = bimolecular, 3 = termolecular.
Check: a one-step mechanism has no intermediate.
tricks: The '2' in SN2 means bimolecular, not two steps.
Carbocation intermediates belong to SN1, not SN2.
if_lost: What does the '2' in SN2 stand for?
How many steps does an SN2 mechanism have?
Which particles collide in that step?

1_context.short: AO1: link a mechanism label to molecularity.
1_context.why: R2.2.8 defines molecularity as the number of particles reacting in an elementary step. SN2 is the standard bimolecular example.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.8: molecularity is the number of reacting particles in an elementary step (uni-, bi-, termolecular).
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach SN2 in the organic chapter. The exam tests it as a kinetics idea.

2_markscheme_logic.short: A: two particles in the single rate-determining step.
2_markscheme_logic.why: In SN2 the nucleophile attacks as the leaving group departs, in one step. Two particles collide, so it is bimolecular.
trigger_phrases: nucleophile and substrate in the rate-determining step
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Use 'unimolecular' or 'bimolecular' for molecularity. 'First order' was accepted once but is not correct (10M.2.HL.TZ1.7).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A versus D: D describes SN1, which goes through a carbocation in two steps.

3_novel_application.short: An organic label hides a kinetics definition.
3_novel_application.why: The question looks like an R3.4 mechanism question but tests R2.2.8 vocabulary.
3_novel_application.avoid: Recalling curly arrows instead of counting particles.
3_novel_application.disguise: A reaction-mechanism name instead of an elementary-step equation.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Count the particles that collide in the slow step.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: one true statement about SN2.
4_command_terms.why: Each distractor matches a different mix-up: steps, the attacking species, or SN1.
4_command_terms.avoid: Choosing the option with the most technical wording.
4_command_terms.demands: Pick the correct statement about SN2 kinetics.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 1 mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.why: A single memorised fact settles it.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No mechanism drawing needed.

6_data_booklet.why: Mechanism names and molecularity terms are not in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.memorise: SN1 is unimolecular via a carbocation; SN2 is a single bimolecular step.

7_elimination.short: B, C and D each describe something that isn't SN2.
7_elimination.why: Each distractor matches a different mix-up: the number of steps, the attacking species, or SN1.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping D because carbocations sound familiar.

definitely_wrong.rule: SN2 is a single concerted step.
In nucleophilic substitution a nucleophile replaces the leaving group.
A carbocation intermediate belongs to SN1.

walkthrough.answer: A. SN2 is a single step in which the nucleophile and the substrate collide, so it is bimolecular.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.2.8: unimolecular, bimolecular and termolecular elementary steps.
1_context.textbook_gap: Molecularity is often taught only in organic chemistry. Exams link it to the rate-determining step and to the order.

trigger_phrases: number of particles in the rate-determining step
trap_boundaries: 'First order' is not the same as 'unimolecular' (10M.2.HL.TZ1.7).
Molecularity applies to a single elementary step, never to the overall equation.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit uses the molecularity term for the step, not the order of the reaction.

disguises: A question about the SN1/SN2 name (25N.1A.HL.6207.40).
A halogenoalkane question asking for the molecularity (10M.2.HL.TZ1.7).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Count the particles that collide in the slow step.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Usually 1 mark for the correct term.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No rate data needed.

6_data_booklet.hack: Molecularity terms are NOT in the booklet.

rules: An elementary step with three or more particles is rare (termolecular); four or more is not credible.
A single-step mechanism has no intermediate.
Molecularity is always a whole number of particles, never zero.

evidence.note: SN2: two molecules in the rate-determining step (A).
Many wrote 'first order' instead of 'unimolecular'; accepted that time, but not correct.

cards.difficulty_signal: Little direct statistical evidence. Terminology confusion was noted in 10M.2.HL.TZ1.7, and SN1 mechanisms were poorly done (03N.3.SL.TZ0.1).

cross_links.note: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally and leaves K unchanged (06M.2.SL.TZ0.6; 08M.2.SL.TZ0.7).
SN1 and SN2 mechanisms give the classic unimolecular and bimolecular rate-determining steps (25N.1A.HL.6207.40; 10M.2.HL.TZ1.7).
Energy profiles and bond strength: exothermic means stronger bonds in the products and a larger reverse Ea (20N.1.HL.TZ0.15).
